name: Breakout Board

claims.claim_text: Small-package adapter boards carry a large price premium relative to the bare silicon they host: a panel of SOT-23 or SC-70 breakouts was quoted at around sixty dollars, which is far more than the parts being adapted.
claims.quote_verbatim: 60 bucks for a sheet of the, of the, uh, SOT 23 breakout, or SC70 breakouts
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - The Ternary Tussle

claims.claim_text: Commercial SOIC-to-header breakout boards can be glued down component-side-up onto an unetched copper-clad sheet and wired freestanding to the surrounding parts, giving a solid ground plane under everything. That construction is a long-standing technique and behaves well at high frequency.
claims.quote_verbatim: So he's done all the components sort of dead, not quite dead bug, cause they're not upside down, but just, uh, freestanding on the copper clad board. And that's a time honored, time honored construction technique. And it's a great high frequency technique.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Chaining a fine-pitch connector into an adapter board that converts it to 0.1 inch adds two extra interfaces and two extra failure points. When board area is not scarce, placing the 0.1 inch header directly on the design is simpler than adapting down to it later.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have the, the real small, the small pitch connectors and then I have a breakout board and then, and then it goes to the, the 0.1 inch.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: A useful class of evaluation board is a breakout that also carries a communication link such as SPI or a serial interface, so a new chip can be dropped onto an otherwise fixed layout, sent to the fab, and exercised over that link without building the rest of a system around it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Basically making like breakout boards that also happen to have, you know, spy and, you know, a serial link, you know, like just a simple link kind of stuff.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: Once fine-pitch surface-mount parts around 0.5 mm pitch are involved, adapter boards for them are only useful if they are already on the shelf. Ordering one specially takes about as long as ordering a purpose-built board that does the whole job, so the adapter stops being a shortcut.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, yeah, you can get breakout boards, but I don't keep those in stock, you know? I've got to, oh, I might as well, you know, by the time I order that, I might as well order a board, you know?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: Charging a premium for a through-hole DIP version of a part drives the low-volume user toward buying the cheap surface-mount version plus an adapter board instead, because the combination still comes out cheaper than the DIP.
claims.quote_verbatim: Paying more money is, eventually you're just going to have someone say, well, I'll just, I'll do a breakout board. I don't care. It's just cheaper.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: DIP projects, OSHW & Trade Booths - Demonstrative DIP Dacrygelosis

claims.claim_text: Development boards and breakout boards are built specifically so another engineer can learn from them or build on them, which is the argument for releasing them under the most permissive licence available. Dangerous Prototypes moved from Creative Commons attribution-share-alike to effectively public domain, retaining only the trademark on the name, to remove licensing friction for users.
claims.quote_verbatim: And this started with development boards and breakout boards because you're making a board specifically for an engineer to use to build or learn a project.
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Breakout boards designed to satisfy one personal project turned into a saleable product line: after building a carrier for a Bluetooth class-2 module for a wearable, demand appeared for boards around the other modules in that family, and the boards themselves were electrically very simple.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are these other modules out here and Hey, people actually want to give me money because I can give them Bluetooth breakout boards
claims.speaker: Jeff Rowberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: Early module carrier designs accumulate mistakes that only become visible with more experience of the module itself, which is why a maker of such boards later goes back and reissues revisions of boards that were already selling.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I actually just went through a round of revisions for some of the breakout boards that I sell
claims.speaker: Jeff Rowberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: Desktop fabrication methods have a floor on package size and cannot handle ball grid arrays, so as packages continue to shrink an adapter board remains necessary to use modern parts with them. For anything beyond a single one-off, even a run of ten, a professionally fabricated FR4 board is the sensible endpoint.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're still going to need some kind of breakout in order to use those boards or use those printers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: One way to make an unusual microcontroller accessible is to build what amounts to an enlarged breakout board around it, adding an expansion interface and a fast USB interface so the part can be used without the user having to solve its board-level problems first.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I'm currently building a board that's basically like a glorified breakout board for the LPC 4300 family just so that people can have this part on an easy-to-use board with an expansion interface and a really fast USB interface.
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: In-house etching and milling processes with roughly a 10 mil feature limit are adequate for many boards but cannot resolve current fine-pitch footprints, so a purchased adapter board becomes a prerequisite for using new parts on home-made PCBs.
claims.quote_verbatim: But, like, any of the new footprints, it's like, no, I mean, like, footprints aren't getting bigger. So, you at least need to have a breakout then.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A structural fix for fine-pitch samples would be for semiconductor vendors to ship free samples already mounted on adapter boards, though sample budgets are exactly where vendors are trying to spend less.
claims.quote_verbatim: the other option there is if, you know, if more chip companies start just attaching samples to breakout boards
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The 1Bitsy is a simple breakout for a higher-end STM32 F4 part, but the interesting engineering sits alongside it in the Black Magic Probe, an open hardware debugger for ARM parts that displaces expensive proprietary debug toolchains.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a pretty simple breakout for a higher-end STM32, like an F4 chip
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: When several breakout modules must sit together in a fixed arrangement, soldering 90 degree headers instead of straight ones gives each module a flat face that effectively surface-mounts to a piece of bare FR4. From there the interconnect is point-to-point wire with discrete parts added in line, and the result is compact, durable, and buildable the same day.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than solder on straight headers, you can solder on 90 degree headers. So they have like a flat side and they just kind of surface mount to a piece of FR4
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Standardising on one keyed 20-pin header, arranged two by ten on 0.1 inch centres so it occupies one inch by 0.2 inch, and carrying two supply rails plus analog inputs, SPI, I2C and serial, covers roughly ninety percent of typical small designs and lets any new circuit or adapter board interoperate with existing ones. Keying the connector prevents it being plugged in reversed.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's keyed in order to, uh, you know, so you can't switch it around and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A reusable header definition should be chosen to span the common interface set rather than one project's needs, so that a single connector handles analog input, SPI, I2C and serial across most boards a designer produces.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically you can handle, I'd say 90% of the stuff that I normally do, you know, analog input, spy, I squared C, serial, stuff like that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Putting the processor on a pluggable module and designing only the carrier board around it isolates the design from obsolescence of that specific module. If the chosen microcontroller board goes end-of-life, or the requirement changes to a wireless variant, the sensor carrier does not have to be redesigned.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I want to switch to Wi-Fi, or if the Teensy 3.2 goes obsolete, and later I switch to something else, basically it doesn't matter
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: Connecting external signals directly to a microcontroller pin without protection is a routine way to destroy the part, so the interesting design question for a carrier or breakout board is which protection measures to add around the exposed pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: people can blow up their micros by hooking shit straight up to the pin
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: A minimal breakout that simply routes the pins of a USB-C physical-layer chip out to 0.1 inch headers is enough to drive the part from an off-the-shelf microcontroller board and prove out an application before committing to a custom PCB.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have a little breakout board that basically breaks the pins of this PHY out to headers. And that's what I used for the USB-C Easy Bake Oven. Just jump it over to an Arduino.
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: The hardware effort in adapting a USB-C PHY is trivial next to the firmware: bringing one up meant porting a library from an existing open embedded codebase and running to somewhere around four thousand lines of code on a small microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was porting a library that Google Chrome has for their embedded computing. And I sort of lost count of the number of lines somewhere around 4,000.
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: On a weight-critical board the ideal interconnect is bare solder pads, but 0.05 inch pitch connectors are already difficult enough for a general audience that dedicated adapter boards were added for specific target vehicles so users could simply plug in. The compromise was made explicit by perforating the tabs around the board so a builder who cares about grams can snap them off.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's trading off weight versus ease of use.
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Working with pre-certified radio modules such as the u-blox parts reduces the electrical work to breaking out the module's pins, since the difficult circuit design is already inside the module.
claims.quote_verbatim: we use, like, U-Blocks modules. They're real simple in terms of, like
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: As more functionality is absorbed into modules, board-level work shifts from designing circuits to producing breakouts that connect modules together, a Lego-block style of assembly. That shift matches what most customers want, since they are trying to finish a product rather than design circuitry.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fact that I'm just going to be doing breakouts for modules, it's not like I'm designing circuits at that point
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Matching the physical size and the power and ground pinout of an established development board lets a new board drop into the ecosystem of carrier boards already built for the original. Signal pins cannot always be matched, so compatibility is partial and must be stated as such.
claims.quote_verbatim: The pinout for power and signals I've kept compatible for power and ground.
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: A carrier board can expose the daughterboard's test points as well as its headers by giving the carrier a footprint for tiny pogo pins that are hand-soldered in place. When the daughterboard is soldered on top, the pogo pins bear against its test pads and bring the programming and debug nets out to the carrier.
claims.quote_verbatim: he has this footprint that allows you to manually solder those little pogo pins, um, on the breakout board. And then when you put the FPGA board on top and you solder it in, all the test points make contact with those pogo pins.
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: A deliberately trivial first board, such as a simple breakout, is the right vehicle for learning a PCB tool, because the point is to build fluency with the software rather than to solve a design problem at the same time.
claims.quote_verbatim: have like one small thing you want to do first. You know. A breakout board or whatever. Just to get started. Just to get used to the keystrokes.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Keeping an in-house etching setup permanently loaded and ready, so that starting it heating is a single button press at the beginning of a layout, changes it from an occasional chore into a same-day process. The workload it actually absorbs is dominated by simple adapter boards, against an alternative wait of two to four days for outside fabrication.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's only, like, really simple stuff, like breakout boards are probably the thing I use it for more than anything else, actually
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A prototype assembled from off-the-shelf breakout boards and plug-in prototyping boards is easy to change, which is the entire point of a prototype, and the wait for a fabricated PCB is spent writing firmware. Services that sell a fast custom prototype PCB by pointing at the unreliable connections of breakout-board prototypes ignore how much back-and-forth a prototype board actually takes.
claims.quote_verbatim: Completely missing that the entire point of a prototype is you can change it easily.
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: An automated PCB design service offering a board in 24 hours for three thousand dollars bounded its scope tightly: on the order of fifty components, twenty unique components, under 250 items, under 3 amps, under 500 megahertz and under 20 watts total.
claims.quote_verbatim: for $3,000 in 24 hours, they'll design your PCB
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Building a breakout board for every component in the working parts library, each breaking out to 0.1 inch pins, makes even sub-millimetre-pitch BGAs usable on a breadboard and stops package choice from silently ruling parts out of a design.
claims.quote_verbatim: basically every component I ended up using, uh, I create a breakout board for it
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: A modern DIP part is itself an adapter: the die inside is tiny and is bonded out to a large lead frame, which is the same conversion a breakout board performs on the outside of the package.
claims.quote_verbatim: even when you buy a dip part these days, it's effectively the same thing. Just internally, they're bonding out the chip, the tiny, tiny bit of silicon up to these huge lead frames.
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: An Ethernet add-on board for a small hardware platform was discontinued after only around fifty units because wired networking drew far too much power for that class of product and because demand was clearly for Wi-Fi and wireless instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: we did an Ethernet shield, which was a bit crazy. Um. And that, we maybe made 50 of them. And that was a, that was a huge pain as we discontinued that.
claims.speaker: Ken Burns

claims.claim_text: Wafer-level chip scale packages are small and light enough that solder surface tension dominates and they self-align much like a passive resistor, whereas ball grid arrays are large enough that surface tension helps considerably less during reflow.
claims.quote_verbatim: WCSP packages are so small and so light and the surface tension is so strong. Um, they act much more like you're soldering things like resistors than they do
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: For a silicon shuttle program aimed at people without fine-pitch assembly capability, one option under consideration is returning fabricated ICs already mounted on breakout boards that expand the die out to a castellated-edge module or even a DIP footprint.
claims.quote_verbatim: we may even go as far as having you get back a bunch of, um, your ICs pre-mounted on these breakout boards that do things like expand it out to a cast related edged, uh, module, or maybe even a dip package
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Building a series of small boards that do nothing beyond booting and presenting a console is legitimate practice, not wasted effort. Ten such boards over six months, running only basic shell commands and a benchmark with no networking, was the deliberate way one engineer learned embedded Linux hardware before trusting the skill on a real product.
claims.quote_verbatim: I built 10 of these boards, spent six months and none of them do a goddamn thing.
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: Web-based carrier-board configurators such as Gumstix Geppetto let a user pick one controller, a limited set of components and modules, and a limited set of connectors, and generate the breakout board for a compute module. The constraint is the narrow parts catalogue, and the alternative of learning a full EDA tool costs well over a thousand dollars of a designer's time.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're allowed to select one controller like an atmel or or whatever it is uh then you're allowed to select components
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Modular design has an optimal granularity. Taking it to the limit with a breakout board per chip does make everything swappable, but the added interconnects and extra PCBs carry real cost, so the design question is where to draw the boundaries rather than how modular to be.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could say like oh well i'm going to use just like breakout boards for every single chip on the board and then everything is super modular and it's like okay that works but then you have in that example you know the added cost of interconnects and extra pcbs
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: When no module existed for a particular radio part, one engineer built a castellated-edge module for it and a matching Feather-format breakout board so the module could drop into other people's designs, publishing the design files and selling low-volume production units. An official vendor module for the same part only appeared about two years later.
claims.quote_verbatim: It made a feather board for it, like a breakout board.
claims.speaker: Orkhan Amiraslanov

claims.claim_text: Low-volume module production moved offshore for price reasons returned roughly ninety percent total yield, which was considered acceptable for an uncertified self-built module.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was the yield total yield was like about 90%
claims.speaker: Orkhan Amiraslanov

claims.claim_text: Instead of hand-wiring off-the-shelf sensor breakout boards together, a very simple custom PCB can replace the point-to-point wiring: the sensor boards keep their 0.1 inch headers and solder into the carrier, so no individual sensors have to be sourced or placed. A five-board run from a low-cost fabricator is the entire production quantity needed for demos.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I'm still buying off the shelf sensor breakout boards, but now I'm just like making it simple to solder them together in what I call like Lego prototyping.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A first spin that does nothing but break out the pins of a part, with a couple of devices hung off the I2C bus, is worth building purely to confirm that the footprint is correct before that footprint propagates into a real design.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I did a breakout. Basically. Just to. I'm just proving out. That I. Have the right footprint.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Centralising the hard parts of a design into one reusable module, with cellular or Wi-Fi and the surrounding support circuitry on a six-layer board, leaves only a two-layer breakout carrying a battery and one sensor. Swapping an accelerometer for a pressure sensor then becomes a trivial board change, and assembly is simplified because the complex board is a single placed part.
claims.quote_verbatim: You kind of centralize the complexity onto the module. In this case, like they had modules, a six layer board, and then there's going to be a two layer breakout board for the little battery plus sensor thing.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Once the complexity is pushed into a module, the simple carrier board can be handed to a separate design team or an outside specialist and plugged in, because the interface between the two is fixed and narrow.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can even give it to a different design team. You can even have somebody else who's an expert in doing that sort of stuff. You can have them develop the little board and then you just plug it in, for example.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A fully modular product built from simple functional boards is really an evaluation-board or demo-board style of product, useful for proving that a module plus a battery plus a sensor is a working thing, rather than an end product architecture in itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're kind of in like the sort of like evaluation board, demo board kind of market where that thing is like kind of handy
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A Bluetooth breakout board around a Nordic part, with battery charging, USB and an LED, thirteen pins down each side on 0.1 inch centres, was three dollars delivered from China. That price is below what the equivalent board can be built and shipped for elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: The board shipped to my house from China was $3.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Nobody is producing a breakout board for a high-end Bluetooth system-on-chip at the two-dollar level in a Western market, because at those prices the margin on the finished board is essentially nothing once postage is accounted for.
claims.quote_verbatim: nobody is making an Android 52 840 breakout board for, you know, $2
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

Passage [8] (ep 125) carries the diarisation label SPEAKER_00, but the content is the guest describing Dangerous Prototypes' own licensing practice ('At Dangerous Prototypes, we try to make a new open source hardware project every month'); attributed to Ian Lesnet by content.
Passage [9] (ep 155) is labelled 'Jeff Roberg', a transcription error for the guest Jeff Rowberg; attributed to Jeff Rowberg.

Passage [11] (ep 265) is labelled Chris Gammell, but the content is the guest describing a board he is personally building for the LPC4300 family ('I'm currently building a board'), which is Michael Ossmann's own work; attributed to Michael Ossmann by content.

Passage [28] (ep 458) is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE. The Ethernet-shield content is the guest describing his own company's discontinued product ('we did an Ethernet shield... we maybe made 50 of them'); attributed to Ken Burns by content. The surrounding Adafruit/SparkFun comparison in the same passage is host commentary and was not used.
Passage [30] (ep 515) is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE. The content is the guest describing his own embedded-Linux write-up and the ten boards he built; attributed to Jay Carlson by content.
Passages [26] and [25] (ep 412) mix host and guest turns; both quotes used are from Mike Harrison's own turns describing his etching setup and his reading of the automated-PCB-design service.

Passage [33] (ep 522) is labelled Chris Gammell in the bundle, but the underlying transcript places the modular-granularity turn under the guest label 'Frederick Kinsander' (a transcription of Fredrik Kensander). The content is generic design reasoning and does not settle which of the two said it, so the speaker is left unset.
